articles.hook: OpenAI just made decision-making fast, cheap, and ridiculously efficient.
articles.headline: OpenAI launches Decisions API for faster, cheaper AI-powered choices
articles.body: OpenAI has released the Decisions API, a new tool designed to help developers build applications that make fast, focused, and cost-effective decisions. The API is engineered specifically for scenarios where applications need to quickly evaluate options and take action without unnecessary computational overhead. Unlike general-purpose language models that can be resource-intensive, the Decisions API strips away complexity to focus purely on decision-making tasks—choosing between options, evaluating conditions, or routing requests based on criteria. This makes it dramatically cheaper to run at scale compared to running full model inference for every decision point. The technology is particularly valuable for applications that make thousands or millions of micro-decisions daily: e-commerce platforms deciding which product to recommend, customer support systems routing tickets to the right team, financial apps evaluating transaction risk, or content platforms filtering user submissions. By offloading decision logic to a specialized, lightweight API rather than building it into custom code or expensive model calls, developers can reduce latency and infrastructure costs simultaneously. The Decisions API represents OpenAI's push into the infrastructure layer, competing with both traditional backend services and other AI providers offering similar decision-making capabilities.
examples: Feed customer data into the API and get instant routing decisions to the best support agent.
Run real-time fraud detection on transactions with sub-millisecond latency and minimal compute cost.
Evaluate user queries and decide whether to use a cheap or advanced model based on complexity.

Instead of building entirely new RL pipelines from scratch, teams can use their current grading systems (pass/fail flags, quality ratings, user feedback stored in databases) to reward or penalize agent actions in real-time. This dramatically reduces the overhead of post-training agents compared to building custom reward models from scratch. The core insight is that most enterprises already have structured feedback in their databases; ThinkingBox makes that feedback immediately actionable for RL training. Early implementations show agents trained this way converge faster and exhibit more robust decision-making on complex reasoning tasks. The approach works with any agent architecture and integrates with existing model training pipelines, making it practical for teams already running inference systems with logged performance data.

The specialized agents handle the actual domain reasoning. This architectural shift has delivered notable improvements in both efficiency and accuracy across Meta's data pipeline agents. The key insight is that centralizing too much intelligence in one place creates bottlenecks and increases failure points. By distributing domain expertise to specialized agents while keeping the routing layer minimal, Meta reduced cognitive load on the orchestrator and improved overall system performance. This approach mirrors established principles from distributed systems and microservices architecture, but applied to AI agent design. For teams building production AI systems, this pattern suggests that agent reliability isn't just about making individual components smarter—it's about designing an orchestration layer that knows exactly what to delegate and when.
